blocks.content: In distributed systems, communication between clients and servers happens over networks, and networks are inherently unreliable. A request may reach the server successfully, but the response can be lost due to a timeout, network failure, or temporary outage.

From the client's perspective, it is impossible to know whether the operation actually executed or not. To improve reliability, clients often retry failed requests. However, retries create a new challenge: the same operation may be executed multiple times.

For read operations, this is usually harmless, but for write operations such as creating an order, processing a payment, or booking a ticket, duplicate execution can lead to serious issues like double charges, duplicate records, or multiple shipments.
To safely support retries without causing unintended side effects, distributed systems rely on the concept of idempotency.
1. What is Idempotency?

Idempotency is the property that calling an operation multiple times produces exactly the same result as calling it once. In distributed systems, the network can drop a response after the server has already acted on the request.
The client retries, thinking the first attempt failed. Without idempotency, the user gets charged twice, the order ships twice, or the record is duplicated.
With idempotency, the second call simply returns the already-computed result as if the first call were the only one.

This lesson covers: what idempotency means, the problem it solves, idempotency keys, server-side deduplication, database-level enforcement, HTTP method semantics, expiry and storage design, and the mistakes that break idempotency guarantees.

blocks.content: 2. The core problem: at-most-once vs at-least-once
blocks.text: 2. The core problem: at-most-once vs at-least-once

blocks.content: Every distributed call falls into one of two delivery guarantees. At-most-once means the operation runs zero or one times if the network drops, the client accepts the loss.
At-least-once means the client retries until it gets confirmation but that creates the risk of the operation running more than once. Idempotency is what makes at-least-once delivery safe for writes.
Without Idempotency

["The client sends a request: \"Charge $100\".","The server receives the request and successfully charges the customer.","Before the response reaches the client, the response is lost due to a network issue.","The client assumes the request failed because it never received confirmation.","The client retries the same request: \"Charge $100\".","The server treats it as a completely new request and charges the customer again."]
items: The client sends a request: "Charge $100".
The server receives the request and successfully charges the customer.
Before the response reaches the client, the response is lost due to a network issue.
The client assumes the request failed because it never received confirmation.
The client retries the same request: "Charge $100".
The server treats it as a completely new request and charges the customer again.

blocks.content: Result: The customer is charged twice even though they intended to make only one payment.
With Idempotency Key

["The client generates a unique idempotency key, for example \"abc\".","The request becomes: \"Charge $100, Key=abc\".","The server processes the payment, stores the result, and associates it with key abc.","The response is lost.","The client retries with the same idempotency key.","The server checks its storage and finds that key abc has already been processed.","Instead of charging again, it returns the previously stored result."]
items: The client generates a unique idempotency key, for example "abc".
The request becomes: "Charge $100, Key=abc".
The server processes the payment, stores the result, and associates it with key abc.
The response is lost.
The client retries with the same idempotency key.
The server checks its storage and finds that key abc has already been processed.
Instead of charging again, it returns the previously stored result.

blocks.content: Result: The customer is charged only once.
3. HTTP method idempotency

The HTTP spec defines which methods are safe to call multiple times. This is the first line of idempotency in any API design choosing the right verb communicates the contract to every caller and every infrastructure layer in between.

["GET; Idempotent and safe.Reads the same data every time. No side effects. Safe to retry unconditionally.
","PUT: Idempotent.Replaces a resource entirely. SendingPUT /orders/42twice with the same body leaves exactly one order in the exact same state.
","DELETE: Idempotent.Deleting something that is already deleted is a no-op. The resource is absent either way same final state.
","POST: Not idempotent by default.Creates a new resource each time. Safe to retry only when the server implements an idempotency key mechanism on top.
","PATCH: Depends on the operation.PATCH balance += 100is not idempotent.PATCH balance = 500is. Design PATCH bodies as absolute replacements, not relative increments, to make them safe to retry.
"]

blocks.content: 4. Idempotency keys
When an operation cannot be made inherently idempotent through its semantics (such as a payment charge via POST), the standard pattern is an idempotency key.
The client generates a unique token before the first attempt and sends it in every retry.
The server stores the result of the first successful execution against that key and returns it on every subsequent call with the same key without re-executing the operation.
Key generation rules

["Generate once, before the first attempt. The key must be stable across all retries of the same logical operation. Generate it at the point you decide to perform the operation, not inside the retry loop.
","Use a UUID v4 or ULID. Cryptographically random, globally unique, no coordination needed. ULIDs have the bonus of being lexicographically sortable by creation time.
","Scope the key to the logical operation. A key for \"charge order #99\" should not be reused for \"refund order #99.\" Each distinct business action gets its own key.
","Never generate a new key inside the retry loop.This defeats the entire purpose each retry would be treated as a fresh first call, and you're back to double-charging.
"]
items: Generate once, before the first attempt. The key must be stable across all retries of the same logical operation. Generate it at the point you decide to perform the operation, not inside the retry loop.
Use a UUID v4 or ULID. Cryptographically random, globally unique, no coordination needed. ULIDs have the bonus of being lexicographically sortable by creation time.
Scope the key to the logical operation. A key for "charge order #99" should not be reused for "refund order #99." Each distinct business action gets its own key.
Never generate a new key inside the retry loop.This defeats the entire purpose each retry would be treated as a fresh first call, and you're back to double-charging.

blocks.content: 5. Server-side deduplication
The server receives the key and must decide: have I seen this key before? If yes, return the stored result.
If no, execute the operation, store the result, and return it. The store must be fast enough to check on every request and durable enough to survive restarts.
6. In-flight deduplication (concurrent same key)
A subtle race: two retries arrive at the server simultaneously, before either has finished executing.

Both check the store, both find nothing, both start executing and you get two charges again. The fix is to lock the key for the duration of the first execution so the second waits and then reads the stored result.

blocks.content: 7. Database-level enforcement
For operations that write to a database, a unique constraint on the idempotency key column is the most reliable safety net.
Even if application logic has a bug that skips the key check, the database will reject the duplicate insert. The unique constraint is the last line of defence.

blocks.content: 8. Key expiry and storage design
Idempotency keys cannot be stored forever the store would grow unboundedly.
The TTL (time-to-live) must be long enough that any realistic retry window fits comfortably inside it, but short enough to reclaim space. A common choice is 7 to 30 days for payment-level operations.
What to store

["The idempotency key itself","The serialised response body","The HTTP status code returned","A timestamp of first execution","The request fingerprint (optional, to detect key reuse with a different payload)"]
items: The idempotency key itself
The serialised response body
The HTTP status code returned
A timestamp of first execution
The request fingerprint (optional, to detect key reuse with a different payload)

["Redis with SET key value EX ttl fast, simple, right for most cases","Database unique column slower but durable across restarts, doubles as audit trail","In-memory map only valid for single-node, single-process, non-persistent scenarios","Avoid: Bloom filters alone (false negatives possible), file system (no atomic check-and-set)"]

Database unique column slower but durable across restarts, doubles as audit trail

Avoid: Bloom filters alone (false negatives possible), file system (no atomic check-and-set)

blocks.content: 9. Payload fingerprinting

What should the server do if the same key arrives with a different payload? The safe answer is to reject it return a 422 or 409 and tell the caller that this key has already been used for a different operation.
This prevents an attacker (or a buggy client) from reusing a key to change the amount of an already-processed charge.
Suppose a client sends:

Key = abc
Amount = $100
The server processes the payment and stores:

• Idempotency Key: abc
  • Fingerprint (hash of the request payload)
  • Result
Later, someone sends:

Key = abc
Amount = $500
using the same idempotency key but with a different payload.
The server checks the stored fingerprint against the new request's fingerprint. If they don't match, it rejects the request with an error such as 409 Conflict or 422 Unprocessable Entity.
This prevents a buggy client or attacker from reusing an old idempotency key to perform a different operation.
In short:

• Same key + same payload → Return the cached result.
  • Same key + different payload → Reject the request.
  • New key → Process normally.
This ensures that an idempotency key always represents one specific operation and one specific payload.
10. Common mistakes

Mistake 1: new key per retry The most common mistake. The key is generated inside the retry loop, so every attempt is a fresh first call. The server sees three different keys, executes three times, and the user is charged three times. Generate the key once, before any attempt.

Mistake 2: no concurrent deduplication Two retries arrive simultaneously. Both check the store and find nothing. Both execute. The unique constraint on the database catches it, but only after both charges have been issued to the payment network. Add a distributed lock (Redis SET NX) to prevent concurrent execution of the same key, not just sequential deduplication.

Mistake 3: no payload fingerprint check Same key, different amount. Without fingerprinting the payload, the server happily charges the new amount and treats it as the cached response for the original key. Always hash the request body and reject mismatches.

Mistake 4: storing keys in memory only An in-memory map works until the server restarts. After restart, the store is empty every previously-seen key looks new, and the next retry causes a duplicate execution. Use Redis or a database for the idempotency store in any production service.

Mistake 5: TTL too short A 60-second TTL means any client that retries after a minute sees a fresh key and causes a duplicate. TTL must cover the entire realistic retry window including backoff, plus a margin. For payment-level operations, 7 days is the industry standard minimum.
11. Quick reference

["Idempotency key UUID generated once per logical operation, before any attempt, sent on every retry as a header or body field.
","Server deduplication Check store on arrival. Cache hit → return stored result. Cache miss → execute, store, return.
","Concurrent safety Redis SET NX lock per key prevents two simultaneous first executions from both slipping through the empty store check.
","Database constraint Unique index on the idempotency key column is the last-resort safety net even if application logic has a bug.
","Payload fingerprint SHA-256 of the canonical request body stored with the key. Reject any replay that arrives with a different hash.
","TTL 7–30 days for payment-scale operations. Must exceed the maximum realistic retry window by a comfortable margin."]
items: Idempotency key UUID generated once per logical operation, before any attempt, sent on every retry as a header or body field.
Server deduplication Check store on arrival. Cache hit → return stored result. Cache miss → execute, store, return.
Concurrent safety Redis SET NX lock per key prevents two simultaneous first executions from both slipping through the empty store check.
Database constraint Unique index on the idempotency key column is the last-resort safety net even if application logic has a bug.
Payload fingerprint SHA-256 of the canonical request body stored with the key. Reject any replay that arrives with a different hash.
TTL 7–30 days for payment-scale operations. Must exceed the maximum realistic retry window by a comfortable margin.
